title: What If You Could Stop Time While Holding Your Breath?

beats.text: box truck glider mot busskuren, 5 inne
Hal ler bakom glaset – han lärde dig
5 personer behöver mer än du klarar
verklig fysik: ljus och ljud stannar
regel 3: du kan flytta det du orkar bära
Dex kör mot rött, sedanen glider
du drar Dex två fot åt sidan
utan korrigering: 10 km fel per dag
Marisol frågar inte hur – hon vill köpa det
dom nivå 4: kraften tar något tillbaka
'Breathe, kid. Never past the edge alone.' (planterat)
dom nivå 6: ingen luft, ingen kraft
du lyfter förarens fot från bromsen
fem personer, ett andetag i taget
Hal sparar platsen längst från vägen

scenes.say: A box truck slides on black ice toward a bus shelter with five people inside.
You breathe in and hold it. Every snowflake on Halsted Street stops in midair.
This is every level of stopping time with one breath, and the science behind it.
The truck is frozen 9 feet from the glass. Your lungs give you about 41 seconds.
That isn't much. Most people manage 30 seconds to a few minutes.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: to a few minutes, for most people
visual.source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ask Smithsonian: What's the longest you can hold your breath?'

scenes.say: Behind the glass, an old man named Hal is still smiling at you, because he taught you this.
On day 1 you couldn't hold it for 40 seconds. Today, five people need you to go longer.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: trained free divers have gone as deep as 700 feet on one breath
fact_strip.source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'What's the longest you can hold your breath?'

scenes.say: So, what if you could stop time, but only for as long as you hold your breath?

visual.text: breathe out, and the world starts again

scenes.say: Day 1 is a Monday in December, at a bike courier depot in Chicago.
Level one is the hiccups, which is how you find out about any of this.

visual.text: THE HICCUPS: 38 seconds of nothing

scenes.say: You've had the hiccups since breakfast, loud ones, and dispatch keeps laughing at you over the radio.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: rarely, hiccups can go on for months

scenes.say: Marisol Vance runs dispatch. She times every delivery with a silver stopwatch and says every second is a dollar.
Here's what a hiccup is. A spasm in your diaphragm makes your vocal cords snap shut, and that makes the sound.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: diaphragm spasm, vocal cords snap shut

scenes.say: So you do what everyone's grandmother tells you to do. You take a big breath, and you hold it.
The radio goes quiet mid-word. Marisol's stopwatch hangs at 14 seconds, and the hiccups are gone.
Nobody in the depot is moving. A coffee is pouring out of a cup and has stopped halfway to the floor.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: a clock's second hand can seem to stand still when you first look at it

scenes.say: For most people, hiccups only last a few minutes. Mayo Clinic says to see a doctor if they last more than 48 hours.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: hiccups longer than that: see a doctor

scenes.say: Your chest starts to burn at about 38 seconds. You gasp, and the coffee hits the floor all at once.
That burn has a real cause. High carbon dioxide, not low oxygen, is what makes a long breath-hold hurt.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: high carbon dioxide drives the burn, not low oxygen
visual.source: Smithsonian Magazine, quoting Mayo Clinic's Dr. Clayton Cowl

scenes.say: Marisol stares at the puddle, then at her stopwatch, then at you, as if the numbers just skipped.
Level one verdict: you can stop the whole world for 38 seconds, and the only price is a burning chest.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: pre-breathing pure oxygen before a hold is 'a bit of a trick'
fact_strip.source: Ohio State Wexner Medical Center, Dr. Jonathan Parsons

scenes.say: Day 3, at home, with the bathroom door locked and a phone stopwatch running.
Level two is the rules, because a power with no rules is going to get somebody hurt.

visual.text: THE RULES: 3 of them

scenes.say: You start the stopwatch on your phone and hold your breath. The stopwatch freezes along with everything else.
So you count in your head instead, one Mississippi at a time, like a kid playing hide and seek.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: light already on its way could reach you for up to 8 minutes after time stopped
fact_strip.source: Discovery, 'What Would Happen If You Stopped Time?'

scenes.say: Rule one: breathe in, and time stops. Rule two: breathe out, and it starts again exactly where it was.
Real physics is much harsher. If time really stopped, physicists point out, all light and sound would stop too.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: if time stopped, both would stop with it
visual.source: Discovery, 'What Would Happen If You Stopped Time?'

scenes.say: Even the air would freeze in place, with every molecule stuck where it is. You couldn't take a single step.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: every molecule held in place, so you couldn't move

scenes.say: In our story, light and air still work for you. That part is made up. Everything on a card like this is real.

visual.text: the power is fiction. the cards are real.

scenes.say: What does feel real is the silence. No traffic, no wind, no radiator, only your own heartbeat.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: with pure oxygen first, a diver held 20 min 21 s in 2010

scenes.say: Rule three you learn by accident. You can move things while time is stopped, but only what you can carry.
Your limit is still 38 seconds, and on days when you're tired it drops to about 30.
Level two verdict: the power is real, it has rules, and the only clock still running is the one in your lungs.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: the record before 2021: 24:03.45, Barcelona, 2016

scenes.say: Day 6, rush hour at Halsted and Madison, and you're racing another courier.
Level three is Dex Moreau, the fastest courier in the depot, and he wants every one of your routes.

visual.text: DEX MOREAU: never brakes

scenes.say: Dex rides an orange bike, never stops at red lights, and has called you Hiccup since Monday.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: 2024: 858 bicyclist deaths in urban areas, 200 in rural

scenes.say: He blows straight through a red light. A sedan is braking hard from the left, and it isn't going to stop in time.
You breathe in and hold it. The sedan stops two feet from Dex, its tires locked on the wet road.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: with ABS: practice NOT pumping the brake

scenes.say: Then you notice something strange. The driver has the steering wheel turned hard right, and the car is sliding dead straight.
That's real. Without antilock brakes, NHTSA says a hard stop can lock the wheels and take away your steering.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: hard braking without ABS can lock the wheels

scenes.say: You can't move a car, but you can move a bike. You drag Dex and his bike two feet to the right.
At 33 Mississippi you breathe. The sedan slides past, and Dex has no idea why he's still alive.
Crashes like this aren't rare. In 2024, 1,075 bicyclists were killed in crashes with motor vehicles in the U.S.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: bicyclists killed in U.S. crashes, 2024

scenes.say: And 81 percent of them were killed in urban areas, on city streets a lot like this one.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: of U.S. bicyclist deaths in 2024

scenes.say: Dex looks at you, pale as the snow, and for the first time he calls you by your real name.
Level three verdict: one breath can save a life, and locked wheels go wherever they want to go.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: in winter, increase your following distance

scenes.say: Day 11, and Marisol calls you into the dispatch office with a printout in her hand.
Level four is Marisol and her stopwatch, because numbers don't lie, and your numbers are impossible.

visual.text: MARISOL VANCE: 1 stopwatch, 0 excuses

scenes.say: Your GPS log shows you three blocks away from a drop-off, and then at the drop-off, with zero seconds in between.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: relativity: satellite clocks lose 7 µs a day to speed, gain 45 µs to weaker gravity
fact_strip.source: Ohio State University, Prof. Richard Pogge

scenes.say: Your phone logged 4:12:07 at Jackson, then 4:12:07 again at Wacker. Same second, three blocks apart.
GPS is fussy about time anyway. Because of relativity, satellite clocks tick about 38 microseconds a day fast.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: per day, GPS clocks vs ground clocks
visual.source: Ohio State University, Prof. Richard Pogge, 'GPS and Relativity'

scenes.say: If nobody corrected for that, GPS positions would drift by about 10 kilometers, roughly 6 miles, every day.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: the error if relativity were ignored
visual.source: Ohio State University, Prof. Richard Pogge, 'GPS and Relativity'

scenes.say: Time really does run at different speeds. In 1971, atomic clocks flown east around the world lost 59 nanoseconds.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: lost by atomic clocks flown east, 1971
visual.source: Hafele & Keating, Science (1972), via HyperPhysics, Georgia State University

scenes.say: Flown west, they gained 273 nanoseconds. Your problem is that you just gained three whole blocks.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: gained flying west

scenes.say: Marisol doesn't ask how you did it. She slides a contract across the desk and asks how much of it you can do.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: 1971: four cesium-beam clocks flew on regular airline flights

scenes.say: Her offer is the rush route. Every package under 15 minutes pays 40 dollars, and the big ones pay 500.
So you start freezing time 30 times a day, and by Friday your pay for the week is 1,840 dollars.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: uncorrected GPS would be wrong after only 2 minutes
fact_strip.source: Ohio State University, Prof. Richard Pogge

scenes.say: You also start getting headaches, and twice this week the edges of the room have gone gray before you breathed.
That's a real warning sign. An Ohio State doctor says that if you hold your breath long enough, you could pass out.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: from holding your breath too long
visual.source: Ohio State Wexner Medical Center, Dr. Jonathan Parsons (2024)

scenes.say: He also says one minute is probably the limit, and that you might reach 90 seconds without getting into trouble.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: probably the limit; maybe 90 seconds
visual.source: Ohio State Wexner Medical Center, Dr. Jonathan Parsons (2024)

scenes.say: Level four verdict: the power pays very well, but every freeze takes a little something back from you.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: predicted in 1971: −40 ns flying east, +275 ns flying west

scenes.say: Day 15, at the Route 8 bus stop on Halsted, at 4:40 in the afternoon.
Level five is Hal Benning, who is 74 and the only person who ever notices you breathing.

visual.text: HAL BENNING: 74, the 4:40 bus

scenes.say: Hal waits for the same bus every day at 4:40. He sees you gasp after a freeze and offers you a mint.
He coached swimming at a YMCA for 40 years, and he says you breathe like a kid who just learned to dive.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: NYC health code requires pool signs warning against hyperventilating

scenes.say: Then he says something that stops you cold. Breathe, kid. Never hold it past the edge, and never alone.
He isn't being dramatic. The CDC found 16 swimmers in New York State hurt in underwater breath-holding incidents, and 4 died.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: dangerous breath-holding, New York State, 1988–2011: 4 died

scenes.say: Breathing fast before a breath-hold lowers your carbon dioxide, so the urge to breathe comes late, and you can black out first.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: lowers CO2, delays the urge, risks blackout

scenes.say: So, for real: never practice holding your breath in water, and never hyperventilate before you try.

visual.text: and never breathe fast first

scenes.say: Hal teaches you on dry land, on the bench, with slow breaths and loose shoulders, and you stop before it hurts.
He also shows you a trick. Cold water on your face can start the diving reflex, which slows the heart 10 percent or more.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: cold water on the face: heart rate down 10% or more

scenes.say: In some marine mammals, that same reflex slows the heart by roughly 90 percent.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: heart-rate drop in some diving mammals

scenes.say: In one week your limit goes from 38 seconds to 1 minute and 25. You still stop the second it starts to burn.
Trained free divers go much further, holding for 4 to 8 minutes or more without breathing oxygen first.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: trained free divers, no oxygen beforehand
visual.source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'What's the longest you can hold your breath?'

scenes.say: In 2009, Stéphane Mifsud held his breath for 11 minutes and 35 seconds, with no pure oxygen beforehand.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: static breath-hold, 2009, no oxygen

scenes.say: The Guinness record is 24 minutes and 37 seconds, set in 2021 in Croatia by a 56-year-old free diver, Budimir Šobat.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: Guinness record breath-hold, 2021

scenes.say: But he breathed pure oxygen before the attempt, which the record's rules allow for up to 30 minutes.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: allowed for 30 minutes before the attempt

scenes.say: Hal hears all of this and says he's 74, his personal record is a nap, and his bus is late again.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: 15 of those 16 incidents happened at New York State bathing facilities

scenes.say: Level five verdict: the power grows with training, and the man who trains you sits in that glass box every day at 4:40.
Day 22, on the icy stairs up to a train platform, with a package in each hand.
Level six is the fall, and it teaches you the one thing your power can't do.

visual.text: THE FALL: 0 seconds of air

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: diving reflex: blood vessels in skin and limbs narrow, saving blood for the core

scenes.say: Your foot hits a patch of ice on the top step, and you go over backward down the stairs.
You try to freeze it, but you just shouted, and your lungs are empty. Time doesn't stop at all.
And yet the fall feels slow. You see every step, every rivet in the railing, and a pigeon taking off.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: divers with experience can strengthen the reflex (2000 study)

scenes.say: You land on a pile of shoveled snow at the bottom, sore but whole, and lie there for a full minute.
That slow feeling has been tested. In 2007, researchers dropped volunteers 150 feet into a safety net.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: free fall into a net, 2007 study
visual.source: National Geographic, on Stetson, Fiesta & Eagleman, PLoS ONE (2007)

scenes.say: People guessed that their own fall had lasted 36 percent longer than the falls they watched other people take.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: how much longer their own fall seemed
visual.source: National Geographic, on Stetson et al., PLoS ONE (2007)

scenes.say: But a flickering number on their wrists was just as hard to read as it was on the ground. Time didn't slow down.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: they read the numbers no better than on the ground
visual.source: National Geographic, on Stetson et al., PLoS ONE (2007)

scenes.say: The researchers think frightening moments leave denser memories, so the moment only seems longer afterward.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: fear makes the moment seem longer later
visual.source: National Geographic, on Stetson et al., PLoS ONE (2007)

scenes.say: Level six verdict: no breath, no power. From now on, before every corner, you keep a full breath ready.
That night Marisol calls. Day 30 has a 500 dollar rush package for Wacker Drive, due at exactly 4:45.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: most black ice forms when temperatures hover around freezing

scenes.say: Day 30, 4:38 in the afternoon, 31 degrees with freezing drizzle, and Halsted is glazed with black ice.
Level seven is the ice, and it's the moment you saw at the very start of this video.

visual.text: THE ICE: 5 people, 9 feet

scenes.say: You're 6 blocks from Wacker with the 500 dollar package, and you sprint the bike the whole way.
Winter driving guides put it plainly. It's harder to control or stop a vehicle on a slick surface, so leave more distance.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: slick roads: harder to control, harder to stop

scenes.say: At Halsted, a box truck brakes for the light, and its back end swings out toward the bus stop.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: black ice: a thin, clear layer of ice on dark asphalt

scenes.say: Hal is in the shelter with four other people: a nurse, a man with groceries, a student, and a mail carrier.
You breathe in and hold it. But you just sprinted 6 blocks, and the burn starts almost right away.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: bridges and overpasses freeze before other surfaces
fact_strip.source: National Weather Service, 'Ice Storms' safety page

scenes.say: You count what you've got. About 41 seconds of air, a truck 9 feet from the glass, and five people inside.
You can't push a truck that weighs as much as a small house. You try anyway, and nothing moves at all.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: a single vehicle rated 26,001 lb or more needs a commercial license

scenes.say: Then you remember Dex and the sedan. The truck's wheels aren't turning, because the driver is standing on the brake.
NHTSA's advice: with antilock brakes, keep firm pressure and steer. Without them, you may need to pump the brakes as wheels lock.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: no ABS: wheels can lock. with ABS: press firmly and steer
visual.source: NHTSA, 'Antilock Brake Systems' and 'Winter Driving Tips'

scenes.say: Locked wheels can't steer. So you climb into the cab and pull the driver's boots off the brake pedal.
Then you turn the steering wheel a quarter turn toward the snowbank, while you count 33 Mississippi, 34.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: cold water on the face: the airway snaps shut, the diving reflex begins

scenes.say: You breathe out. The world jumps forward one second, and the truck slides one more foot toward the glass.
You breathe in again. Now the wheels are rolling, and the truck has started to turn, but not fast enough.
In breath-hold blackouts, the CDC says the cause is the oxygen in your arteries dropping too low.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: caused by arterial oxygen dropping too low

scenes.say: Its back corner will still clip the shelter, right where Hal is sitting with his paper bag of mints.
Hal is a big man, and dragging him across the ice will take longer than your lungs can last.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: black ice is often clear, with the black road visible underneath
fact_strip.source: National Weather Service, 'Ice Storms' safety page

scenes.say: So you have a choice. Hold past the edge alone and maybe black out, or breathe and give the truck another second.

visual.title: THE CHOICE
lines: A: hold past the edge, alone

scenes.say: You hear Hal's voice in your head, and it's annoyingly calm. Breathe, kid. Never past the edge alone.
So you breathe after every 20 Mississippi. Each breath, the truck slides a few inches. Each freeze, you drag Hal a little farther.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: black ice also forms on sidewalks, steps and decks

scenes.say: Doctors compare the last stage of a very long breath-hold to a kind of carbon dioxide narcosis, a foggy, heavy feeling.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: how a very long breath-hold can feel
visual.source: Smithsonian Magazine, quoting Mayo Clinic's Dr. Clayton Cowl

scenes.say: The ice helps here. Hal slides like a sofa on a polished floor, out of the shelter and into the snow.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: underpasses shade the road and keep it from warming

scenes.say: Then the nurse, then the man with the groceries, then the student, then the mail carrier, one breath at a time.
On the last breath you let go. The truck rolls into the snowbank, and the shelter glass cracks with nobody inside.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: black ice is most common in the early morning hours
fact_strip.source: National Weather Service, 'Ice Storms' safety page

scenes.say: Hal sits up in the snow, looks at the empty shelter, then at you, and says it one more time. Breathe, kid.
You reach Wacker Drive at 4:49 with the package. Marisol's silver stopwatch says you're exactly 4 minutes late.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: the 24:37 record was set in Sisak, Croatia, on 27 March 2021

scenes.say: She says the rush route needs someone who never misses a deadline. You slide the contract back across her desk.
Dex takes the rush route. On his first day he stops at a red light, and he waves at you with his whole arm.
The 2024 total of bicyclist deaths was the third-highest number IIHS has ever recorded.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: U.S. bicyclist deaths, 2024

scenes.say: And every day at 4:40, Hal saves you the seat at the end of the bench, the one farthest from the road.
Hal, Marisol, Dex and the frozen truck are made up. The breathing, the brakes and the clocks are all real.

visual.text: the power and the people are fiction. the facts are real.

scenes.say: And one more time, because it's real: never practice breath-holding in water, and never on your own.

visual.text: never alone

scenes.say: Your turn. On day 30, would you hold past your limit to save Hal faster, or breathe every 20 seconds like he said? A or B.
Level 8 is coming next. What if the Earth stopped spinning, for just one second?
And tonight, look at a clock with a second hand. That first tick can seem to hang, by up to half a second.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: the first second you see can last up to 0.5 s longer

scenes.say: That's chronostasis, the closest any of us will get to stopping time, and you don't even have to hold your breath.

seo.hook: A box truck is sliding on black ice toward a bus shelter with five people inside. You breathe in and hold it. Every snowflake on Halsted Street stops in midair.
seo.summary:
What if you could stop time, but only for as long as you can hold your breath? Breathe in and every snowflake on the street hangs in the air. Breathe out and the world starts again. You're a bike courier in Chicago in December, and in 30 days you find out the rules, save a rival from a skidding sedan, get paid to freeze time 30 times a day, learn to breathe from a 74-year-old swim coach at a bus stop, and fall down an icy staircase with empty lungs. On day 30 a box truck slides on black ice toward a bus shelter with five people inside, and you have about 41 seconds of air.

This is a fictional What If story. The power and every character (Hal, Marisol, Dex) are made up. The facts on screen are real:
- Most people can hold their breath for 30 seconds to a few minutes; trained free divers 4–8 minutes or more; high carbon dioxide, not low oxygen, drives the burn (Smithsonian Magazine, quoting Mayo Clinic's Dr. Clayton Cowl)
- A hiccup is a diaphragm spasm that snaps the vocal cords shut; see a doctor after 48 hours (Mayo Clinic)
- "One minute is probably the limit"; holding too long can make you pass out (Ohio State Wexner Medical Center, Dr. Jonathan Parsons)
- Diving reflex: cold water on the face can slow a person's heart 10% or more, roughly 90% in some marine mammals; Stéphane Mifsud 11:35 in 2009 (Scientific American)
- Guinness record 24:37.36 by Budimir Šobat, 56, Sisak, Croatia, 27 March 2021, after breathing pure oxygen (Guinness World Records)
- Dangerous underwater breath-holding, New York State 1988–2011: 16 swimmers, 4 deaths; hyperventilating first lowers CO2 and risks blackout (CDC MMWR, 2015)
- If time truly stopped, light, sound and air would stop too (Discovery, quoting physicist Sean Carroll)
- GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast; uncorrected, positions would drift about 10 km a day (Prof. Richard Pogge, Ohio State)
- Hafele–Keating 1971: atomic clocks lost 59 ns flying east and gained 273 ns flying west (HyperPhysics)
- Volunteers dropped 150 feet guessed their fall lasted 36% longer, but time didn't slow down (National Geographic, on Stetson, Fiesta & Eagleman, PLoS ONE 2007)
- Without ABS, hard braking can lock the wheels and take away steering (NHTSA); slow down and leave more distance on slick roads (NHTSA Winter Driving Tips)
- 1,075 U.S. bicyclists killed in crashes with motor vehicles in 2024, 81% in urban areas (IIHS)
- Black ice is thin, clear ice on dark asphalt; bridges and overpasses freeze first (National Geographic, National Weather Service)
- Stopped-clock illusion (chronostasis): the first second you see can seem up to half a second longer (Wikipedia)

Never practice holding your breath in water, never hyperventilate first, and never do it alone.

seo.question: On day 30, would you hold past your limit to save Hal faster, or breathe every 20 seconds like he said? A or B.
seo.pinned_comment: A or B: hold past your limit to drag Hal out faster, or breathe every 20 seconds like he told you? Level 8 is coming: what if the Earth stopped spinning for one second?
seo.playlist: What If You Could...? Hypothetical Scenarios

thumb.script: huvudchatten bygger (thumbs_v3_all.py-stil; ny plats halsted_street + frozen=True)
thumb.klickfraga: Tiden står still bara så länge han håller andan – lastbilen hänger 9 fot från en busskur med fem personer, och han har 41 sekunder luft. Hinner han?
thumb.hot_i_bild: En stor box truck som sladdar snett i bild på blank svart is, fryst mitt i rörelsen med snöflingor som hänger i luften, och hörnet bara en meter från en glasbusskur med fem personer – lastbilen tar ~45 % av bilden (vänster–mitten).
thumb.skiljer_sig: Förra TLI (tli-2026-11-21) var ett vertikalt hotelltorn med röken uppe till vänster och text nere till vänster. Nu: horisontell vintergata i dagsljus, hotet (lastbilen) i vänster–mitten, hjälten lugnt gående i förgrunden till höger med kinderna fulla av luft, gul text uppe till höger. Ny effekt: frusna snöflingor/blåaktig ton = superkraften syns i bild.
thumb.forsta_scen_matchar: Scen 1 (0–7 s) är A-miniatyren i rörelse: samma Halsted-gata i ljust vinterdagsljus, box trucken sladdar på svart is mot busskuren med fem personer (threat=truck_skid, drive_to). Scen 2 (7 s) fryser samma bild: snöflingorna stannar (frozen=True, tystnad). HUD 'AIR 0:41' = miniatyrens siffra.

forbattring.forra_videon: tli-2026-11-21 'What If You Could Never Forget Anything for 30 Days?' (MANUS KLART 21/11, publiceringsstatus saknas i kö.md) och senast publicerade OOBnQjk7zV0 '1850' – 0 exponeringar (KANALANALYS_2026-11-22).
forbattring.matt_forra: TLI: 0–1 exponeringar per lång video; ingen tittarkurva än (TITTARTID_ANALYS_2026-11-22).
forbattring.problem: Distribution: titlarna har inte varit exakta sökförslag och kanalen har inga Shorts. Innehåll: tidigare TLI-manus hade verkliga fakta bara på 12 kort (en var ~75:e s) och långa stämningsstretcher – förlorarmönstret i TITTARTID_ANALYS.
forbattring.andring: TITTARTID_REGLER: TRENDORDER (titeln innehåller förslag nr 1 'what if you could stop time'), INNEHÅLLSORDER (DUI-mallen på What if: 7 numrerade nivåer med dom, en verklig fakta med källa på skärmen minst var 30:e s – 33 THAT'S REAL-kort + 28 faktaremsor + 2 säkerhetskort, största lucka 29,9 s, snitt 19 ord/replik, 0 repliker < 6 ord), FORMATORDER/TLI-raden (sökfras-titel) och DISTRIBUTIONSORDER 2 (första TLI-Shorten).
forbattring.forvantat: Exponeringar via sök på 'what if you could stop time' och via Shorten (mål ≥ 300 första veckan), CTR ≥ 3 %, ≥ 55 % kvar vid 0:30 och ≥ 35 % vid 2:00.
forbattring.referens: DOOMPERK 'What If You Had Infinite IQ in PRISON?' (X_wiaDTxSho, 894 932 visningar på 8 dagar, läst 17 nov) + trenden 22 nov: ConChaser 'What If You Could See Everyone's IQ?' 2 898 995 (månad), What If Effect 'What If You Were Born With Infinite IQ?' 890 222 (vecka).
forbattring.vi_slår_den_med: Kraften har en fysisk mätare som tittaren känner i sin egen kropp (håll andan medan du tittar), varje nivå lär ut en verklig sak om andning, tid eller is med källa, och klimaxet löses av två planterade fakta (låsta hjul kan inte styra – nivå 3; Hals regel 'never past the edge alone' – nivå 5) i stället för av kraften.
forbattring.trend: Ämne/titel ur TREND_2026-11-22 (TLI): 'What If You Could …'-superkraft. Sökförslag: 'what if you could stop time' (förslag nr 1, trend/tli.json). Trendande videor: ConChaser 'What If You Could See Everyone's IQ?' 2 898 995 visningar (månad), 'What If You Could See Everyone's Future Wealth?' 2 388 323 (månad), What If Effect 'What If You Were Born With Infinite IQ?' 890 222 (vecka). Ingen video med exakt vår titel hittad (webbsök 22/11); 'What If You Could Stop Time but Only for 1 Second' finns – vår begränsning (andan) är en annan.

standard_check.miniatyr: A: kraften som siffra '41 SEC' i stor gul text (TLI_STANDARD 6), lugn hjälte på väg framåt, 5 bifigurer i kuren med uppspärrade ögon, ljus vinterdag. B = fråga, C = HUD 'AIR 0:41'.
standard_check.krok: 0 s hotet (lastbil mot kur, 5 personer), 7 s kraften visas (andas in – snön stannar, tystnad), 12 s löftet i klartext ('every level of stopping time with one breath, and the real science of holding it'), 19 s insatsen med siffror (9 fot, 41 s) = slutlöfte, 26 s första verkliga faktakortet, 34 s gåtan (Hal lärde dig), 49 s titelfrågan. Ingen presentation före första händelsen.
standard_check.nivåer: LEVEL 1 The hiccups · 2 The rules · 3 Dex · 4 Marisol (stopwatch/GPS) · 5 Hal · 6 The fall · 7 The ice · Level 8: ??? (what if Earth stopped spinning). Dom efter varje nivå.
standard_check.verkligt_faktum_per_nivå: 1: Mayo hicka ×2, Smithsonian CO2 · 2: Discovery ljus/ljud/luft · 3: NHTSA låsta hjul, IIHS 1 075 / 81 % · 4: GPS 38 µs/10 km (Pogge), Hafele–Keating 59/273 ns, OSU svimning/1 min · 5: CDC 16/4 + hyperventilation, dykreflex 10 %/90 %, fridykare 4–8 min, Mifsud 11:35, Guinness 24:37 + rent syre · 6: Eagleman 150 ft / 36 % / läste inte snabbare · 7: NHTSA vinter + ABS, CDC blackout, CO2-narkos, svart is (NatGeo/NWS), FMCSA 26 001 lb · Slut: IIHS 3:e högsta, kronostas.
standard_check.planteringar_som_betalas: 1) Låsta hjul kan inte styra (nivå 3, Dex) → klimax: foten av bromsen + ratten · 2) Mississippi-räkningen (nivå 2) → '33 Mississippi, 34' och '20 Mississippi' · 3) Hals regel 'Breathe, kid. Never past the edge alone' (nivå 5) → valet · 4) Hal i glaslådan kl 4:40 (nivå 5) → busskuren dag 30 · 5) Marisols stoppur (nivå 1) → 4 minuter sen · 6) $500-paketet 4:45 (nivå 6) → valet pengar mot människor · 7) tomma lungor = ingen kraft (nivå 6) → sprinten tar luften dag 30. Återkommande skämt: 'Hiccup' / Hals mint.
standard_check.känsloslag: Dex säger ditt namn, Hal ler bakom glaset, 'Breathe, kid.' i snön, Hal sparar platsen längst från vägen.
standard_check.moraliskt_val: Mitt i: Marisols rush route ($40/$500) – kraften för pengar. Klimax: hålla förbi gränsen ensam (snabbare, risk för blackout) eller följa Hals regel; och $500-paketet mot fem personer. Speglar kroken.
standard_check.slut: Fråga A/B till tittaren + fäst kommentar, 'Level 8: ???', ett verkligt fenomen att prova i kväll (kronostas) och säkerhetskortet.
standard_check.HUD: DAY x / 30 · AIR (0:38 → 1:25 → 0:41 efter sprinten) · PAY ($0 → $1 840 → $4 100) på varje bild.
standard_check.bilder: Wide första 30 s (0 medium), 8 närbilder (ingen före 2:15), 3 tavlor, 4 ritningar, 33 THAT'S REAL-kort, scene-andel 47%. Tystnad (silence) vid varje frysning som är en vändning.
standard_check.innehall: Snitt 19.1 ord per say; 0 say under 6 ord; faktaskyltar på skärmen: 33 THAT'S REAL-kort + 28 faktaremsor (fact_strip) + 2 säkerhetskort = 63; största lucka mellan två faktaskyltar 29,9 s. Löftet i klartext vid 0:12. Högst ett icke-progressivt moment per nivå (hicka/skratt, tystnaden, 'Hiccup', –, Hals tupplur, –, soffan på isen).

experiment.variable: titel = exakt sökförslag nr 1 + faktaskylt var 30:e s + första TLI-Shorten

notes.påhittat: Kraften (tiden stannar medan du håller andan), alla personer (Marisol Vance, Dex Moreau, Hal Benning, föraren, de fem i kuren), budfirman, alla belopp ($40, $500, $1 840, $4 100), klockslag, avstånd (9 fot) och andningstiderna 38 s / 1:25 / 41 s. Halsted, Madison, Jackson, Wacker och busslinje 8 Halsted är verkliga gatunamn i Chicago men inget som händer där är verkligt.
notes.verkligt: Bara THAT'S REAL-korten, faktaremsorna och säkerhetskorten. Verkliga personer (Budimir Šobat, Stéphane Mifsud, Sean Carroll, Richard Pogge) nämns bara på faktakort, aldrig i påhittade scener.
notes.research: vidIQ 0 krediter (återställs 23 nov 19:29 UTC). Ingen Chrome i molnkörningen → youtube-transcriber gick inte; TubeAlfred-nyckel saknas. Topplistan kommer från GitHub Action niche-trends (trend/tli.json i repot, 22 nov 03:05): ConChaser 'See Everyone's IQ?' 2 898 995 (mån), 'Future Wealth?' 2 388 323 (mån), What If Effect 'Born With Infinite IQ?' 890 222 (vecka), What1fy 'Pick Your Speed Every Morning?' 486 397 (vecka). Inget transkript i dag – krokens 0/5/10/20/30 s är från TLI_STANDARD (DOOMPERK, läst 17 nov): 0 s premiss + orättvisa, ~5 s kraften visas, ~10 s vändningen, ~20 s en regel som låter som visdom, ~30 s målet + tidslinjelöften. Källor öppnade 22 nov via web-fetch: Smithsonian, Mayo Clinic, OSU Wexner (health.osu.edu), Scientific American, Guinness 2021, CDC MMWR mm6419a3 + erratum mm6425a6, Discovery, Wikipedia Chronostasis, Pogge (Ohio State), HyperPhysics, National Geographic (Eagleman 2007; black ice 2026), NHTSA ABS + Winter Driving Tips, IIHS Fatality Facts 2024, NWS Ice Storms, FMCSA CDL. PLoS ONE-originalet (PMC2110887) blockerades av reCAPTCHA – siffrorna 150 ft/36 % är från National Geographics genomgång. Wikipedia anger kronostas 'upp till en halv sekund' med Yarrow et al. 2006 som källa (inte 2001).
krokvarianter: A (VALD – visuell, fungerar utan ljud, matchar miniatyren): 'A box truck is sliding on black ice toward a bus shelter with five people inside.' + 'You breathe in and hold it. Every snowflake on Halsted Street stops in midair.'
B (kraften först): 'You can stop time. The catch is that it only lasts as long as you can hold your breath, and you just ran six blocks.'
C (tittaren deltar): 'Take a breath and hold it. Right now. However long you last is how long you'd get to stop the world.'
notes.hook_writer: social-media-skills:hook-writer laddades inte i denna körning (tidsgräns mot render 13:47); tre varianter skrevs enligt TLI_STANDARD 2 och A valdes för att den matchar miniatyren och syns utan ljud.
notes.humanizer: humanizer:humanizer-reglerna tillämpade på alla say-repliker (inga tankstreck, 'truly'/'quietly'/'actually' bort, inga 'not X but Y' utom där källan själv rättar en vanlig missuppfattning (CO2, inte syrebrist)); siffror, källor och fakta oförändrade.

Rekvisita: box_truck (skid, wheels='locked', steer, drive_to), sedan (skid, wheels, steer, drive_to), bus_shelter, snow_frozen, measure (text '9 FT'/'8 FT'), coffee_frozen/coffee_splash, phone (screen), count_bubble (text), window_city, bike, packages (flying), pigeon, snowpile, pedal (pressed), steering_wheel (turn), people_moved (n), snowbank, sink, street_clock. Kläder: hjälten outfit courier + cykelhjälm + budväska (ritas ovanpå, figurkoden orörd); Marisol dispatch + headset + stoppur; Dex orange_courier + orange cykel; Hal ymca_jacket, age='old', keps, mintpåse. NYTT FÄLT visual.fact_strip {head, text, source}: nedre tredjedel med 'THAT'S REAL' + text + SOURCE-rad (samma stil som real-kortets källrad) på 28 scener – den räknas i INNEHÅLLSORDER 2 och MÅSTE ritas, annars blir faktaluckan > 30 s. HUD som 21/11 (dacli2.hud) med a=['AIR', 'm:ss'] och b=['PAY', '$x']. Inga fallbacks till city_street för halsted_street/bus_shelter – miniatyrens scen måste synas i första bilden.
